blocks.text:
Design a Chess Game for two players, White and Black, on a standard 8x8 board. The system must validate that every move follows the moving piece’s own movement rules, prevent a player from leaving their own king in check, and alternate turns correctly.

  • Actors: two players, White and Black, alternating turns.
  • Scope: a full 8x8 board, piece-specific movement validation, capture, and check detection.
  • Goal: guarantee only genuinely legal moves are ever applied, and that a move exposing your own king is always rejected.

The one rule this entire system exists to enforce: a move is only legal if it matches the piece’s own movement shape, does not capture a friendly piece, and does not leave the mover’s own king in check. Every other requirement builds on top of that.

items: The system shall maintain an 8x8 board of pieces belonging to two colors.
The system shall validate that a requested move matches the specific piece’s allowed movement shape.
The system shall reject a move that would capture a piece of the same color.
The system shall reject a move that would leave the moving player’s own king in check.
The system shall alternate turns strictly between White and Black.
The system shall support undoing the most recent move.

metadata.alt: Four non-functional priorities: correctness, extensibility, undoability and performance

items: Correctness: only genuinely legal moves may ever be applied to the board, this is the single most important property of the whole system.
Extensibility: adding a new piece type (or a new rule like castling) must not require changing existing piece classes.
Undoable: any applied move must be cleanly revertible, both for check-testing and for a real undo feature.
Performance: move validation must stay fast even though check detection scans the entire board.
Thread Safety: two rapid move submissions must never corrupt the shared board state.
Do we need to support the full official rule set (castling, en passant, pawn promotion), or a representative subset for this design?
Should checkmate and stalemate detection be fully implemented, or is basic check detection sufficient to demonstrate the core design?
Is this a two-human game, or do we also need to support a computer opponent?
Do we need move history export (like standard chess notation) for replaying games later?
Should the board support loading a game from a saved position rather than always starting fresh?
This design implements King, Rook and Bishop fully, the same Strategy-pattern approach extends directly to Queen, Knight and Pawn.
Castling, en passant and pawn promotion are intentionally out of scope for the core implementation, discussed as follow-up work.

Checkmate and stalemate detection are not implemented, only the core "is the king currently in check" check, since full checkmate detection requires evaluating every legal response, a meaningfully larger algorithm.
The board is a single in-process instance, not persisted between runs by default.
Two human players alternate turns, there is no AI opponent in this design.

metadata.alt: ChessGame composing a Board and a MoveCommand history, with the Board holding a grid of Piece objects

items: Position: a simple row/column coordinate on the board.
Piece: the abstract base every piece type extends, each knows only its own movement rule.
Board: the 8x8 grid of pieces, plus helper queries like path-clearance and attack detection.
MoveCommand: one requested move, capable of both applying and reverting itself.
ChessGame: the top-level orchestrator managing turn order, move validation, and check detection.

metadata.alt: ChessGame composing the Board, which aggregates King, Rook and Bishop pieces

items: Composition: ChessGame composes its Board, the board has no meaningful existence outside a specific game.
Aggregation: Board aggregates the Piece objects placed on it, pieces can conceptually be captured (removed) without the board itself ceasing to exist.
Inheritance: King, Rook and Bishop all inherit from the abstract Piece base, sharing color and the isValidMove contract.
Association: MoveCommand is associated with a specific Board instance and two Position values, but does not own the board’s lifecycle.

metadata.alt: Piece as the abstract base for King, Rook and Bishop, tied together by Board, MoveCommand and ChessGame

blocks.text: Notice that Piece itself has no movement logic at all, every concrete subclass supplies its own isValidMove(). This is deliberate, and is exactly what section 9 covers next.
Three patterns keep this design correct and genuinely extensible.

metadata.alt: Each piece type providing its own movement validation behind the shared Piece contract

blocks.text: Why needed: every piece type moves completely differently, a King and a Rook have nothing in common in HOW they move. Why best: ChessGame never needs to know which specific piece it is dealing with, it only ever calls piece.isValidMove(). What it solves: keeps each piece’s movement rule isolated and independently testable, adding Queen or Knight later means adding one new class, not touching existing ones.

metadata.alt: A MoveCommand executing a move, then being undone if it would leave the mover’s own king in check

blocks.text: Why needed: testing "would this move leave my king in check" requires actually applying the move to see the resulting board, then reverting it if it turns out illegal. Why best: MoveCommand bundles exactly the state needed to reverse itself (the moved piece and whatever it captured), no separate undo bookkeeping needed elsewhere. What it solves: makes speculative moves safe, apply, check, and cleanly roll back if needed.

metadata.alt: PieceFactory creating the correct concrete piece from a type name and color

blocks.text: Why needed: setting up the board (or later, loading a saved game from a compact text notation) needs to turn a piece type name into the right concrete class. Why best: centralizing creation in PieceFactory means adding a new piece type only requires one new case here, not scattered "new XyzPiece()" calls throughout the codebase. What it solves: decouples "which class to instantiate" from every place that needs a piece created.

items: Piece: responsibility is knowing its own color and its own movement rule. Attributes: color. Methods: getColor(), isKing(), isValidMove() (abstract).

Board: responsibility is holding the grid and answering structural questions (is this path clear, is this square attacked). Attributes: an 8x8 grid of Piece. Methods: placePiece(), getPiece(), movePiece(), isPathClear(), findKing(), isSquareAttacked().
MoveCommand: responsibility is applying and reverting exactly one move. Attributes: board, from, to, movedPiece, capturedPiece. Methods: execute(), undo().
ChessGame: responsibility is enforcing turn order and overall move legality. Attributes: board, currentTurn, history. Methods: makeMove(), isKingInCheck(), getCurrentTurn().

metadata.alt: Piece as the single abstraction every concrete piece type implements

blocks.text: The Piece abstraction is the entire design’s extension point for new movement rules. Every future piece type (Queen, Knight, Pawn) needs only to implement isValidMove(), nothing about Board, MoveCommand, or ChessGame ever needs to change.
Three workflows matter most: a move that succeeds, a move rejected purely on shape, and a move rejected because it would expose the king.

metadata.alt: A rook moving in a straight line, passing check detection, and the turn switching to the opponent

blocks.text: This is the full happy path: the piece belongs to the current player, its shape check passes, executing it does not expose the mover’s own king, and the turn switches.

metadata.alt: A king attempting an illegal two-square move, rejected immediately by its own isValidMove check

blocks.text: Shape violations are the cheapest to reject, they never even touch the board, isValidMove() alone is enough to say no.
12.3 A Move Rejected by Check Detection
blocks.content: 12.3 A Move Rejected by Check Detection

metadata.alt: A move that passes its shape check but is undone after discovering it would leave the mover’s own king in check

blocks.text: This is the more expensive rejection path: the move is actually applied, the king’s safety is checked against every opposing piece, and if unsafe, the MoveCommand undoes itself before the illegal move is ever visible to the players.

metadata.alt: The full validation chain: ownership, shape, capture rule, then check safety, before a move is finally applied

items: Happy path: the moving piece belongs to the current player, its shape check passes, the destination is not a friendly piece, and the resulting position does not leave the mover’s own king in check.
Failure, wrong turn: attempting to move a piece of the wrong color for the current turn is rejected immediately.
Failure, friendly capture: attempting to move onto a square occupied by your own piece is rejected before the board is ever touched.
Failure, self-check: a move that is otherwise shape-legal but would expose your own king is applied, detected, and reverted, never left visible on the board.
ChessGame.makeMove(Position from, Position to): the single entry point for attempting a move, returns whether it succeeded.
ChessGame.isKingInCheck(Color color): reports whether the given color’s king is currently under attack.
ChessGame.getCurrentTurn(): reports whose turn it currently is.
Board.isSquareAttacked(Position target, Color byColor): the core query check detection is built on.

metadata.alt: A position outside the 8x8 board being rejected before any board logic runs

items: Invalid input: a Position outside the 0-7 row/column range should be rejected before any board indexing is attempted, to avoid an out-of-bounds error.
Resource unavailable: not directly applicable to an in-memory board, but a persisted variant would need to handle a failed load of a saved game gracefully.
Business-rule violation: PieceFactory.createPiece() throws immediately on an unrecognized piece type, rather than silently returning something incorrect.
System failure: if history tracking itself fails (e.g. out of memory on a very long game), the current board state must remain valid and playable regardless.

metadata.alt: Two move submissions from the same player racing to mutate the shared board and turn state

blocks.text: makeMove() reads and writes the shared Board and currentTurn together, if two calls (accidental double-submission, or two client connections for the same player) run concurrently, the turn-check and the actual move application can interleave incorrectly. The entire makeMove() call must be synchronized (a synchronized method in Java, a threading.Lock in Python, a std::mutex in C++) so no two move attempts are ever processed simultaneously.

items: Adding Queen, Knight and Pawn requires only new Piece subclasses implementing isValidMove(), plus new PieceFactory cases, zero changes to Board, MoveCommand or ChessGame.
Supporting castling would extend MoveCommand to optionally move a second piece (the rook) atomically alongside the king, still within the same execute()/undo() shape.
Supporting pawn promotion would add a branch in MoveCommand’s execute() that swaps the piece type on arrival at the final rank, again without touching other piece classes.

Future work: full checkmate/stalemate detection would layer a "does the current player have any legal move at all" search on top of the existing isKingInCheck() and makeMove() machinery, a meaningfully larger algorithm reusing everything already built here.
Single Responsibility: Piece subclasses only know movement shape, Board only knows grid state, ChessGame only knows turn order and overall legality.
Open/Closed: new piece types and new move types (castling, promotion) can be added without modifying existing, already-correct piece classes.
Liskov Substitution: any Piece subclass can stand in wherever a Piece is expected, ChessGame and Board never need to know which concrete type they are holding.
Interface Segregation: Piece exposes exactly the one method every subclass genuinely needs, isValidMove(), nothing more.
Dependency Inversion: Board and ChessGame depend on the abstract Piece type, never on King, Rook, or Bishop directly.
A move where from and to are the same square: the "no movement" case must be explicitly rejected by each piece’s shape check.
A move that would be shape-legal but the path is blocked by another piece (for Rook and Bishop): isPathClear() must catch this before the move is ever considered legal.
A player attempting to move a piece that is not theirs: rejected at the very first ownership check, before any movement logic runs at all.

Two kings ending up positioned such that neither can safely move without exposing the other, a legitimate but unusual position that check detection alone (without full checkmate search) will not fully resolve.
isValidMove() for King/Rook/Bishop: O(1) for King, O(board size) for Rook/Bishop’s path-clearance scan, so O(8) in practice on this board.
isSquareAttacked(): O(64) in the worst case, checking every square on the board against the target position.
makeMove(): dominated by isSquareAttacked() during check detection, so effectively O(64) per attempted move.
Space: O(1) additional space per move beyond the fixed 8x8 board, plus O(history length) for the undo stack.

metadata.alt: GAME tracking its PLAYER rows and a full MOVE history for replay and analysis

blocks.text: Even though a single game runs in memory, persisting completed games is valuable. GAME stores one row per game with its current status and turn, PLAYER links each color to a real user, and MOVE records the full move history in order, enough to reconstruct and replay any game afterward.

items: How would you implement full checkmate and stalemate detection on top of the existing check-detection machinery?
How would you add castling and en passant without breaking the existing MoveCommand undo guarantee?
How would you support a computer opponent, and where would that logic plug into this design?
How would you extend this design to support online multiplayer with reconnection and move replay?

codes.python:
# Command pattern: a move is captured as an object that can both execute
# and undo itself, essential for safely testing "would this leave my king in check"
class MoveCommand:
    def __init__(self, board, from_pos, to_pos):
        self.board = board
        self.from_pos = from_pos
        self.to_pos = to_pos
        self.moved_piece = None
        self.captured_piece = None

    def execute(self):
        self.moved_piece = self.board.get_piece(self.from_pos)
        self.captured_piece = self.board.get_piece(self.to_pos)
        self.board.move_piece(self.from_pos, self.to_pos)

    def undo(self):
        self.board.place_piece(self.from_pos, self.moved_piece)
        self.board.place_piece(self.to_pos, self.captured_piece)

items: Why does Board expose isSquareAttacked() as a generic query rather than ChessGame directly checking each opposing piece itself? Because "is this square attacked" is a board-level structural fact, keeping it on Board lets both check detection and any future move-legality feature (like castling through check) reuse the exact same query.
Why does MoveCommand need to remember the captured piece, not just the moved one? Because undo() must restore BOTH squares correctly, the destination square is not always empty before the move.

Why is checkmate detection deliberately excluded from this core implementation? Because it requires exploring every legal response the player has, a materially larger search algorithm, isolating it keeps the core move-legality design clean and independently understandable.
An alternative could represent the board as a flat 64-element array instead of an 8x8 grid, marginally simpler indexing math, at the cost of less readable row/column access throughout the codebase.

A simpler design could skip the Command pattern and just simulate a move with a temporary board copy for check-testing, avoiding execute/undo bookkeeping, at the cost of copying the entire board on every single move attempt.

Using bitboards (a real technique from production chess engines) would make move generation and attack detection dramatically faster at large scale, at the cost of far less readable code, not a good fit for a teaching-oriented LLD design.
Persist the move history (already modeled via the MOVE table) so games can be resumed after a disconnect or server restart.
Validate every move server-side even if a client also validates locally, never trust a client to enforce game rules.
Add rate limiting on move submission per player to prevent a buggy or malicious client from flooding makeMove() calls.
Expose a read-only board snapshot API separately from makeMove(), so spectators or replay tooling never risk mutating game state.
